paras: The whipping of Lorenzo Williams was an assault on a Black man by two sons of John T. Phillips near Norway, South Carolina, on Saturday, June 27, 1903, after Williams was accused of swearing at one of them. The Columbia State's correspondent presented it as the start of the trouble that ended four days later in the lynching of Charles Evans, a friend of Williams who had protested the whipping.

Writing from Norway on July 1, Randolph W. Smith of the State said the trouble began over "a comparatively small matter" on the previous Saturday morning. He set it against a complaint that Black people near Norway had been "very trifling and impertinent" and that many had refused to work in the fields.

According to the State, Lorenzo Williams, whom the correspondent called "a negro with a bad reputation," swore at Addie Phillips, a son of John T. Phillips. Phillips consulted friends, who agreed this was "going a trifle too far" and advised him to whip Williams. With the help of his brother, known as "Judge" Phillips, he gave Williams what the correspondent said "everybody in the community" thought he deserved, "a thrashing."

Charles and Jim Evans, two brothers described as friends of Williams, followed him to the place of the whipping. When the elder Phillips brother began to use the lash they protested, and were told that unless they minded their own business they would get into trouble themselves. The Evans brothers left, and some Black residents whom the paper called loyal to their employers later said the two had returned that evening and threatened the whole Phillips family.

Within days John T. Phillips was mortally wounded by a hidden gunman, and early on July 1 the people of Norway lynched Charles Evans, whom they blamed for the shooting. No report of any arrest or charge against the Phillips brothers for the whipping appears in the coverage, and nothing further about Williams was found.

The whipping is known only through the State correspondent's story, which the Union Times reprinted in full on July 3 under the headline "Maddened Citizens Avenge the Crime." The Newberry Herald and News ran a condensed version the same day, saying only that one of Phillips' boys had whipped "a negro named Williams for swearing at him." A rewritten version headed "An Assassin Dies," which dated the whipping June 27, appeared in the Batesburg Advocate and the Manning Times on July 8 and the Marlboro Democrat on July 10.

In every version the whipping served as the motive for the shooting of Phillips, and the correspondent framed both it and the lynching as deserved, writing that no lynching had come "so near justifying the crime." No account of the whipping was found in the Black press, whose Norway items concerned the lynching of Charles Evans and its aftermath, and no version from Williams himself appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Whipping of Lorenzo Williams
bases: Two white brothers, on the advice of friends, summoned a Black man and whipped him for allegedly swearing at one of them; no organized band, night riding or warning is described, so 'whitecapping' does not fit (A1, A2).
Every account traces to one correspondent, Randolph W. Smith of the Columbia State, reprinted or rewritten in other South Carolina weeklies (A1, A2, A5, A6); no independent report was found.

accounts.label: Columbia State correspondent (Randolph W. Smith)
accounts.gist: Williams swore at Addie Phillips; the Phillips brothers, advised by friends, gave him the thrashing the community said he deserved, and warned off the Evans brothers when they protested. The story is told as the start of the trouble that ended in the lynching of Charles Evans.

accounts.label: Black informants (as reported by the State)
accounts.gist: Some Black residents described as 'loyal' to their employers said the Evans brothers came back that Saturday evening and threatened the whole Phillips family.

framing.detail: The State's correspondent wrote that the community said Williams 'deserved' the thrashing, called him 'a negro with a bad reputation', and opened by saying the circumstances came 'so near justifying' the lynching that followed.
Other South Carolina weeklies ran the State story, condensed ('One of Phillips' boys whipped a negro named Williams') or rewritten under 'An Assassin Dies'.

sources.note: Opening of Randolph W. Smith's Columbia State story (Norway, July 1): Lorenzo Williams swore at Addie Phillips on Saturday; Phillips's friends advised him to whip Williams; cut off mid-sentence.
quotes: So on Saturday last when Lorenzo Williams, a negro with a bad reputation, swore at Addie Phillips, a son of John T. Phillips.
The negroes in the vicinity of Norway have been very trifling and impertinent for some time past.
Whatever may be the merits or demerits of lynch law there perhaps never was an instance before where the circumstances came so near justifying the crime.
